pos: n. (the south-western English county, Celtic in speech until the eighteenth century, which rose against the English Prayer Book in 1549 and was never given a Bible in its own tongue)
etymology: Old English Cornwealas, the Welsh of the Corn peninsula, from the tribal name Cornovii and wealas, foreigners; the Cornish called it Kernow.
biblical_def: Cornwall is the peninsula at the south-western end of England, Celtic in blood and in speech, which kept its own Brittonic language in the western hundreds until the eighteenth century. Its Reformation is the dark counterpart to the Welsh. When the Act of Uniformity imposed the English Prayer Book at Whitsun 1549, the Cornish rose; the rebels' articles complained that certain of them understood no English, and the rising was put down with great slaughter at Clyst and in the siege of Exeter. No Cornish Bible was ever made. Where Wales received the Scriptures in its own tongue in 1588 and was reformed by them, Cornwall received a liturgy in a language many of its people could not follow, and the Cornish tongue died without ever carrying the Word. The consequence was a long spiritual dearth, with a scattered and badly served clergy across enormous moorland parishes, until the Methodist preaching of the seventeen-forties onward took hold among the tinners and fishermen as it took hold nowhere else in England. The dictionary records the 1549 rising as a judgment on English policy and not as a defence of the mass, and refuses to call the imposition of an unintelligible service a reformation of worship.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a liturgy as the established form of public worship; uniformity as sameness of form; dearth as scarcity; a tinner as one who works in tin mines; and to understand as to comprehend the meaning of.
webster_full: LITURGY, n. In a general sense, all public ceremonies of divine worship; particularly the established formulas of a church.
UNIFORMITY, n. Sameness of form; conformity to one rule or mode; agreement in form or manner.
DEARTH, n. Scarcity; as a dearth of corn; want; need; famine.
TINNER, n. One who works in the tin mines; one who deals in tin or tin plate.
UNDERSTAND, v.t. To have just and adequate ideas of; to comprehend; to know the meaning of.
scriptures: Yet in the church I had rather speak five words with my understanding, that by my voice I might teach others also, than ten thousand words in an unknown tongue.
So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.
Amo 8:11
Behold, the days come, saith the Lord GOD, that I will send a famine in the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD:
Hos 4:6

My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge: because thou hast rejected knowledge, I will also reject thee, that thou shalt be no priest to me: seeing thou hast forgotten the law of thy God, I will also forget thy children.
corruption_summary: Celtic-speaking south-western county that rose against the English Prayer Book in 1549 because many of its people could not follow it, and which never received a Bible in Cornish before the language died.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption named here is our own, and it is the exact mirror of what the dictionary praises in Wales. Parliament required the Welsh Bible in 1563 and Wales was made Protestant by it; the same state imposed on Cornwall a service in English and answered the protest with soldiers. Paul's rule governs the case and was simply disregarded: “in the church I had rather speak five words with my understanding, that by my voice I might teach others also, than ten thousand words in an unknown tongue” (1Co 14:19). An unintelligible liturgy in English is under the same condemnation as an unintelligible liturgy in Latin, and the dictionary will not exempt it because the men who framed it were Protestants. Faith is not conveyed by sound, for “faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Rom 10:17), and hearing means hearing something understood.

The second paragraph names the consequence, which was famine. Amos foretells a want that is not of bread, “but of hearing the words of the LORD” (Amo 8:11), and that is a fair description of two centuries in the Cornish moorland parishes, enormous, poor and served by men who seldom preached. Hosea states the mechanism without mercy: “My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge” (Hos 4:6), and he lays the charge on the priest who rejected knowledge rather than on the people who lacked it. When the Methodist preachers came among the tinners and the fishermen in the seventeen-forties they were not bringing a novelty into a Christian county; they were bringing the preached Word into a place that had been administered for two hundred years and taught for very few of them.

pos: n. (the large south-western English county of Exeter and the Channel ports, which withstood the 1549 rebels and burned Agnes Prest in 1557)
etymology: Old English Defnas, from the British tribal name Dumnonii; the shire name is Defenascir.
biblical_def: Devon is the great county between Cornwall and Somerset, holding the cathedral city of Exeter, the Channel ports of Plymouth and Dartmouth and the north-coast harbours. Its Reformation history turns on two events. In 1549 the western rebels, chiefly Cornish but joined by men of east Devon, besieged Exeter for five weeks; the city held for the crown and the new service, and the siege was raised in August. Eight years later, under Mary, Agnes Prest, a poor woman of Boyton, was tried for denying that Christ's natural body was in the sacrament and burned outside Exeter in 1557; Foxe records her examination, in which she answered the bishop's chaplains out of the Scriptures and was reckoned mad because she would not retract. Devon men went out to sea in great numbers under Elizabeth, and Plymouth was the port from which the Leiden congregation sailed in 1620. The county's dissent was strong after the Great Ejection, and Exeter's own assembly was the scene of the Arian controversy of 1719 that split the western Presbyterians. The dictionary records the martyr before the admirals and holds that a poor woman's confession at a stake is the county's chief ornament.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a martyr as one who suffers death for his religion; a stake as a post set in the ground; recantation as the retracting of a declaration; a confession as an acknowledgment; and a siege as the surrounding of a place by an army.
webster_full: MARTYR, n. One who suffers death in defence of the Christian faith, or in defence of any cause which he believes to be true.
STAKE, n. A small piece of wood sharpened and set in the ground; the post to which one condemned to be burnt was fastened.
RECANTATION, n. The act of recanting; a retraction of a former declaration or opinion.
CONFESSION, n. Acknowledgment; the acknowledgment of a crime or fault; a profession of belief.
SIEGE, n. The setting of an army around or before a fortified place, for the purpose of compelling the garrison to surrender.
scriptures: Rev 6:9
And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held:
They were stoned, they were sawn asunder, were tempted, were slain with the sword: they wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins; being destitute, afflicted, tormented;
Mat 5:10
Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death.
corruption_summary: South-western county whose city of Exeter held against the western rebels in 1549 and outside whose walls Agnes Prest was burned in 1557 for denying the corporal presence in the sacrament.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the doctrine for which Agnes Prest was killed, the claim that the natural body of Christ is corporally present under the species of bread, and the dictionary names it by its name, transubstantiation, defined at the Fourth Lateran Council and enforced in England by burning. A poor and unlettered woman of Boyton saw through it on the plain ground that a body cannot be in heaven and in ten thousand places at once, and she died for the seeing. John's vision assigns her her place: “I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held” (Rev 6:9). The dictionary does not call her death a tragic consequence of religious division; it calls it a murder done for a false doctrine.

The second paragraph is against a modern softening that is kinder to the persecutor than to the martyr, treating the Marian burnings as an excess of an age rather than the enforcement of a teaching. Scripture gives the sufferers a catalogue and a verdict: “They were stoned, they were sawn asunder, were tempted, were slain with the sword” (Heb 11:37), and the Lord Himself pronounces, “Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake” (Mat 5:10). The victory is located where Prest located it, in the blood of another and in a testimony held to the end, for “they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death” (Rev 12:11). Devon sent out famous seamen; it sent up one better witness.

pos: n. (the western English county of Wells and Glastonbury, which gave its name to the Baptist Somerset Confession of 1656 and rose for Monmouth in 1685)
etymology: Old English Sumorsaete, the dwellers at Somerton, from sumor, summer, and saete, settlers.
biblical_def: Somerset is the county between the Bristol Channel and the Dorset downs, holding the cathedral at Wells, the great abbey at Glastonbury and the levels drained around Sedgemoor. Glastonbury was the richest Benedictine house in England and the last abbot, Richard Whiting, was hanged on the Tor in 1539. The county's importance in the dictionary is twofold. It gave its name to the Somerset Confession of 1656, a confession of sixteen General and Particular Baptist congregations in the west, subscribed by Thomas Collier and others, which set out in plain articles the order of a gathered church, the baptism of believers and the discipline of members. And in 1685 it was the ground of Monmouth's rebellion: the duke landed at Lyme, was proclaimed king at Taunton, and his largely nonconformist following of weavers and farm men was destroyed at Sedgemoor in July, after which Judge Jeffreys hanged and transported them by the hundred in the Bloody Assizes. The dictionary honours the confession and refuses the rebellion, holding that a church may be gathered by profession and that a crown may not be taken by the sword.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a confession of faith as a summary of articles of belief; to contend as to strive in argument; discipline as instruction and correction; rebellion as open resistance to lawful authority; and an assize as a court session.
webster_full: CONFESSION, n. In theology, a formulary of articles of faith; a creed to be assented to.
CONTEND, v.i. To strive or exert against difficulty; to struggle in argument; to dispute earnestly.
DISCIPLINE, n. Instruction and government; subjection to laws and rules; correction; chastisement.
REBELLION, n. An open and avowed renunciation of the authority of the government to which one owes allegiance.
ASSIZE, n. A court in England held in every county by judges of the superior courts; the time or place of holding it.
scriptures: Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican.
Rom 13:1
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
My son, fear thou the LORD and the king: and meddle not with them that are given to change:
corruption_summary: Western county of Wells and Glastonbury, which gave its name to the Baptist Somerset Confession of 1656 and whose nonconformist weavers were destroyed with Monmouth at Sedgemoor in 1685.
corruption_paragraphs: The honourable part of the county's record is the confession, and the dictionary states the principle it rests on. A gathered church confesses a faith in articles because the faith is a definite deposit and not a temper: Jude bids his readers “earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3), and a congregation that will not write down what it holds cannot contend for it. The Somerset men also set out discipline, which is the half of church order most easily let go; the Lord's own direction ends in the congregation, for if an offender “neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican” (Mat 18:17). Sixteen western congregations subscribing one statement in 1656 is the dictionary's pattern of association without prelacy.

The corruption to name is the rebellion, and the dictionary names it against men it otherwise honours. Monmouth's following was largely dissenting, drawn from the very congregations the confession had gathered, and they rose because the law had treated them cruelly. The cruelty was real and the rising was still sin. Paul leaves no room for the calculation they made: “Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God” (Rom 13:1), and Solomon forbids the alliance by its plainest name, “fear thou the LORD and the king: and meddle not with them that are given to change” (Pro 24:21). Sedgemoor and the Bloody Assizes cost the west its best men and gained nothing, and the dictionary records that a persecuted church which takes up arms has exchanged a testimony for a quarrel.

pos: n. (the southern English county whose Dorchester minister John White organised the first Puritan settlement of New England's Cape Ann)
etymology: Old English Dornsaete, the settlers about Dorn, the British name underlying Dorchester; the shire is Dornsaetescir.
biblical_def: Dorset is the southern county of chalk downs and the Channel coast, holding Dorchester, Sherborne, Lyme and the Isle of Purbeck. Its place in the dictionary is the work of one minister. John White, rector of Holy Trinity in Dorchester from 1606 until his death in 1648, made that town a model Puritan borough with a free school, a brewhouse whose profits went to the poor, and a congregation under close catechising; and in 1623 he gathered the Dorchester Company, which planted a fishing and farming settlement at Cape Ann in New England. That settlement failed as a venture and was moved to Naumkeag, which became Salem, and White's company was reorganised into the New England Company and then into the Massachusetts Bay Company. He never crossed the sea himself. Lyme Regis was later the landing place of Monmouth in 1685, and the county suffered in the assizes that followed. The dictionary records Dorset as a place from which men were sent rather than one to which they came, and marks that the organiser of the greatest Puritan emigration stayed at his post in an English parish for forty-two years.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a plantation as a colony or the place colonised; a sojourner as a temporary resident; to emigrate as to remove from one country to another; a company as an association for a common purpose; and a call as a divine summons.
webster_full: PLANTATION, n. The act of planting or setting in the earth; a colony; the place planted or settled.
SOJOURNER, n. One who dwells in a place for a time; a temporary resident; a stranger or traveller.
EMIGRATE, v.i. To quit one country or region and settle in another; to remove from one place to another.
COMPANY, n. An assemblage of persons; a number of persons united for the same purpose, as in trade.
CALL, n. A divine summons or invitation; the summons to the ministry or to a particular work.
scriptures: Gen 12:1
Now the LORD had said unto Abram, Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house, unto a land that I will shew thee:

These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.
Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, to the strangers scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia,
Act 16:9
And a vision appeared to Paul in the night; There stood a man of Macedonia, and prayed him, saying, Come over into Macedonia, and help us.
corruption_summary: Southern county whose Dorchester rector John White built a model Puritan borough and in 1623 gathered the company whose Cape Ann plantation became Salem and then the Massachusetts Bay venture.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a call to send is not a lesser call than a call to go. John White organised the emigration that peopled New England and spent his own life in one Dorset parish; the modern instinct would read that as a failure of nerve or a want of conviction, and the record will not support the reading. He was presented to Holy Trinity in 1606 and buried from it in 1648, and in between he catechised a town, founded its school, endowed its poor out of a brewhouse and corresponded across an ocean. Abraham's call was to go, “Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house” (Gen 12:1); the Macedonian vision came to a man already in the work, and it said “Come over into Macedonia, and help us” (Act 16:9), which is a summons to an errand and not a verdict on those who remain.

The second thing to recover is the settlers' own description of themselves, which was not that of founders. The company that went to Cape Ann failed; the plantation was moved to Naumkeag; the men who crossed expected to be buried in a strange country without seeing what they had attempted completed. Hebrews gives them their proper name, that they “confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth” (Heb 11:13), and Peter addresses a whole dispersion the same way, writing “to the strangers scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia” (1Pe 1:1). A colony conceived as a pilgrimage will outlast a colony conceived as an inheritance, and the dictionary holds that the difference was visible in Dorchester before it was visible in Salem.

pos: n. (the Somerset county town, held for Parliament through three sieges, pastored by Joseph Alleine and the place where Monmouth was proclaimed king)
etymology: Old English Tantun, the town on the river Tone; the river name is British.
biblical_def: Taunton is the chief town of Somerset, standing in the vale of Taunton Deane. In the Civil War it declared for Parliament in a country largely royalist and was besieged three times; Robert Blake, afterwards the Commonwealth's greatest admiral, held it through the winter and spring of 1644 and 1645 against repeated assault and refused summons after summons, and the town was all but destroyed around him. After the war Joseph Alleine came as assistant to the vicar George Newton and served the town from 1655, catechising house by house across the parish and preaching at five in the morning; he was ejected in 1662, imprisoned at Ilchester for preaching, and died in 1668 at thirty-four. His Alarm to the Unconverted, published after his death, went through edition after edition and was one of the most widely read books of English dissent. In 1685 Monmouth was proclaimed king in the market place, and after Sedgemoor the assizes fell on the town heavily. The dictionary sets the pastor above the admiral and the duke, and holds that a parish catechised house by house is a stronger work than a town held through three sieges.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to catechise as to instruct by question and answer; an alarm as a summons to arms or a notice of danger; to eject as to turn out; a course as a race or career; and to persevere as to persist in a design.
webster_full: CATECHISE, v.t. To instruct by asking questions and correcting the answers; to instruct in the principles of religion.
ALARM, n. Any sound, outcry or information intended to give notice of approaching danger; a summons to arms.
EJECT, v.t. To throw out; to cast forth; to dispossess of an office or benefice.
COURSE, n. A running; a race or career; the ground run over; progress; the order of succession.
PERSEVERE, v.i. To persist in any business or enterprise undertaken; to pursue steadily any design.
scriptures: I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith:
Fight the good fight of faith, lay hold on eternal life, whereunto thou art also called, and hast professed a good profession before many witnesses.
Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching.
Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
corruption_summary: Somerset county town held for Parliament through three sieges by Robert Blake, catechised house by house by Joseph Alleine until his ejection in 1662, and where Monmouth was proclaimed king in 1685.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that pastoral labour is measured in households and not in occasions. Alleine had seven years in Taunton and spent them on a method: the town divided, the families visited, the catechism heard, and preaching at five in the morning so that working men could come before their work. Then he was ejected, imprisoned, and dead at thirty-four, and what he left was a parish that had been taught and a book that did the same thing for strangers. Paul's account of his own ending fits the shape of it exactly, “I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith” (2Ti 4:7), and the charge that precedes it is to “Fight the good fight of faith, lay hold on eternal life” (1Ti 6:12).

The second word is about the gatherings the law tried to break, and the dictionary speaks it as a matter of plain duty. The Conventicle Acts made it criminal for the ejected to meet their people, and the ejected met them, in houses, barns and woods, at the cost of fines and gaol. Hebrews forbids the alternative in terms that admit no exception for inconvenience or illegality: “Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is” (Heb 10:25). Where the magistrate commands what God forbids the apostolic answer is the only answer, “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29), and the dictionary marks the difference between that answer and the one the town gave in 1685. Alleine disobeyed a statute and kept preaching; Taunton proclaimed a king and lost its men at Sedgemoor.

pos: n. (the Dorset abbey town and ancient West Saxon see, whose townsmen bought their abbey church at the Dissolution and kept it)
etymology: Old English scir burne, the clear stream, from scir, bright or clear, and burna, a brook.
biblical_def: Sherborne is the Dorset town that was the seat of the West Saxon bishops from 705, when Aldhelm was made bishop of the western half of Wessex; the see was later divided and finally moved to Old Sarum, leaving Sherborne with a great Benedictine abbey. Two churches stood on the one site, the monks' abbey and the townspeople's parish church of All Hallows, and the arrangement produced a famous quarrel in 1437 in which a parishioner's arrow or a plumber's brazier set the abbey roof alight and burned much of the building; the scorched stone is still visible in the vaulting. At the Dissolution in 1539 the abbey was surrendered and the town bought the abbey church outright and pulled down its own smaller one, so that the townsmen ended with the finer building. The school was refounded by Edward VI in 1550. Sir Walter Raleigh held the castle and estate from 1592. The dictionary records the purchase as the best outcome available from a bad transaction, and marks the difference between a house dissolved for its revenues and a church kept for its use.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an abbey as a monastery; dissolution as the act of breaking up; to surrender as to yield up; a sanctuary as a sacred place; and reverence as fear mingled with respect.
webster_full: ABBEY, n. A monastery or society of persons of either sex, secluded from the world and devoted to religion.
DISSOLUTION, n. The act of liquefying; the breaking up of an assembly; destruction of any connected system.
SURRENDER, v.t. To yield to the power of another; to give or deliver up possession upon compulsion or demand.
SANCTUARY, n. A sacred place; particularly among the Israelites, the most retired part of the temple.
REVERENCE, n. Fear mingled with respect and esteem; veneration; awe of the divine.

Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?
Ezr 3:12

But many of the priests and Levites and chief of the fathers, who were ancient men, that had seen the first house, when the foundation of this house was laid before their eyes, wept with a loud voice; and many shouted aloud for joy:
Psa 74:7
They have cast fire into thy sanctuary, they have defiled by casting down the dwelling place of thy name to the ground.
Hab 2:20
But the LORD is in his holy temple: let all the earth keep silence before him.
corruption_summary: Dorset town and ancient West Saxon see whose abbey burned in a quarrel with its own parishioners in 1437 and whose townsmen bought the abbey church at the Dissolution and kept it for the parish.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the Dissolution as it was actually conducted, and the dictionary names it without pretending the monasteries were innocent. The houses were suppressed, their lands sold and their plate melted, and the proceeds went to the crown and to the gentry rather than to preaching, schools or the poor; the reform that was pleaded for was not the reform that was carried out. Haggai's rebuke falls on exactly this order of priorities, asking “Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?” (Hag 1:4). The psalmist's lament over a sanctuary handled roughly is not a defence of the monks' religion but a warning about the handling: “They have cast fire into thy sanctuary” (Psa 74:7), and Sherborne's own vaulting had been scorched once already in 1437 by a quarrel among Christians.

The second paragraph records what was done well here, because the dictionary is bound to say so. The town did not loot the abbey; it bought the church and used it, and demolished its own lesser building rather than keep two. That is the right instinct about a building: it is for the worship of God by a congregation, not a monument to be venerated or a quarry to be stripped. Ezra marks the mixed feeling proper to such a moment, when the old men who had seen the first house “wept with a loud voice; and many shouted aloud for joy” (Ezr 3:12), grief and gladness together. And the rule for what is to happen inside the walls, whoever built them, is Habakkuk's: “But the LORD is in his holy temple: let all the earth keep silence before him” (Hab 2:20).

Hebrew hekal (H1964) — a large building, a temple; “But the LORD is in his holy temple”, Habakkuk 2:20.

pos: n. (the north Devon port on the Taw, a Parliamentarian town in the Civil War and an embarkation point for New England)
etymology: Old English Beardastapol, probably the staple or post of Bearda; the final element is stapol, a pillar or market post.
biblical_def: Barnstaple is the north Devon port standing at the head of the Taw estuary, one of the oldest boroughs in England and for centuries the trading town of the north-west peninsula. Its ships went to Ireland, to Spain and across the Atlantic, and from the sixteen-twenties onward it was one of the west-country ports from which men and families took passage for New England; its merchants fitted out for the Newfoundland fishery as well. In the Civil War the town declared for Parliament, was taken by the royalists, retaken, and finally held by Sir Richard Grenville until 1646; the parish register records the plague and the sieges together. Martin Blake, vicar from 1628, was sequestered by Parliament and then restored, and his long trouble is a fair example of how little either side trusted a moderate. The dictionary records Barnstaple as a place of embarkation, and takes the occasion to set the two ways a man may go to sea: Jonah paid his fare to flee from the presence of the LORD, and others shipped out under a commission to preach to every creature.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a port as a harbour; to embark as to go on board a ship; fare as the price of passage; a commission as a warrant conferring authority; and to enlarge as to extend in limits.
webster_full: PORT, n. A harbour; a haven; any bay, cove or inlet of the sea where ships can lie safe from storms.
EMBARK, v.i. To go on board a ship; to engage in any affair or enterprise.
FARE, n. The price of passage in a ship, coach or other conveyance; money paid for conveyance.
COMMISSION, n. A warrant or written authority conferring power to act in a particular station or employment.
ENLARGE, v.t. To make greater in quantity or dimensions; to extend in limits or breadth.
scriptures: Jon 1:3

But Jonah rose up to flee unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD, and went down to Joppa; and he found a ship going to Tarshish: so he paid the fare thereof, and went down into it, to go with them unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD.
And he said unto them, Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature.
Psa 2:8
Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance, and the uttermost parts of the earth for thy possession.
Isa 54:2
Enlarge the place of thy tent, and let them stretch forth the curtains of thine habitations: spare not, lengthen thy cords, and strengthen thy stakes;
corruption_summary: North Devon port on the Taw, held and retaken in the Civil War, and one of the west-country harbours from which families took passage for New England and the Newfoundland fishery.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that leaving a place is a moral act and takes its character from what a man is leaving it for. Barnstaple sold passages to both kinds of traveller. Jonah's voyage is described with a care that makes the point unmistakable, for “Jonah rose up to flee unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD, and went down to Joppa; and he found a ship going to Tarshish: so he paid the fare thereof” (Jon 1:3); the ship was available, the fare was payable, and the whole arrangement was flight. Against that stands the commission, “Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature” (Mar 16:15), which sends men over the same water on the opposite errand.

The second thing to recover is the breadth of the promise the emigrant ought to have in view. The temptation of a colonial venture is to think in acres and cargoes, and the port of Barnstaple existed to serve exactly that kind of thinking; what Scripture holds out is a possession measured differently, “Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance, and the uttermost parts of the earth for thy possession” (Psa 2:8). The command that follows for those who believe it is one of expansion rather than consolidation, bidding a man “lengthen thy cords, and strengthen thy stakes” (Isa 54:2). A tent with longer cords needs stronger pegs, and the dictionary reads that as the plain condition of any enlargement: new ground requires deeper holding, and a settlement that stretches without strengthening comes down in the first gale.
roots_summary: Hebrew barach (H1272), to flee; Greek kerusso (G2784), to preach as a herald; Hebrew rachab (H7337), to enlarge.

Hebrew sakar (H7939) — wages, hire, a fare; “so he paid the fare thereof”, Jonah 1:3.
Greek kerusso (G2784) — to proclaim as a herald, to preach; “and preach the gospel to every creature”, Mark 16:15.
Hebrew nachalah (H5159) — an inheritance, a possession; “the heathen for thine inheritance”, Psalm 2:8.
Hebrew rachab (H7337) — to be or make wide, to enlarge; “Enlarge the place of thy tent”, Isaiah 54:2.

“preach the gospel to every creature” (Mar 16:15) — the opposite errand over the same water.
“lengthen thy cords, and strengthen thy stakes” (Isa 54:2) — the condition of any true enlargement.

pos: n. (the Cornish shire town on the edge of its moor, mustering place of the risings of 1497 and 1549)
etymology: Cornish Bosvenegh, the dwelling of monks, from bos, a dwelling, and a form meaning monks; anglicised as Bodmin.
biblical_def: Bodmin is the old shire town of Cornwall, standing at the south-western edge of the great granite moor that bears its name, and its name means the dwelling of monks; it held the shrine of Petroc and an Augustinian priory. Twice it was the mustering place of a Cornish rising. In 1497 Michael An Gof, a Bodmin blacksmith, and the lawyer Thomas Flamank led the county out against Henry VII's taxation; they marched to Blackheath and were defeated and executed. In 1549 the Prayer Book rebels gathered there, drew up their articles, and marched east to the siege of Exeter; the provost marshal Anthony Kingston afterward hanged the mayor of Bodmin and others about the county in a progress of summary executions. The dictionary records both risings and judges them separately. The first was a protest against a tax and is judged by the law that forbids sedition; the second was raised in defence of the mass and is judged by the doctrine. What the dictionary will not do is pretend that the reprisals were justice, or that hanging a mayor at his own door was the enforcement of a reformation.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a muster as an assembling of troops; sedition as a commotion in a state; reprisal as the seizing of something in retaliation; summary as done quickly and without ceremony; and zeal as passionate ardour.
webster_full: MUSTER, n. An assembling of troops for review or for service; the register of troops mustered.
SEDITION, n. A factious commotion of the people; a tumult; an insurrection against lawful authority.
REPRISAL, n. The act of taking from an enemy by way of retaliation or indemnity for an injury.
SUMMARY, a. Reduced into a narrow compass; short; done without the usual forms and delay of law.
ZEAL, n. Passionate ardour in the pursuit of any thing; ardent and eager desire, in a good or bad cause.
scriptures: Luk 9:55
But he turned, and rebuked them, and said, Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of.
Jam 1:20
For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God.
Then said Jesus unto him, Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.
(For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds;)
corruption_summary: Cornish shire town on the edge of its moor, mustering place of the 1497 tax rising and the 1549 Prayer Book rebellion, whose mayor was hanged at his own door in the reprisals that followed.
corruption_paragraphs: Two corruptions stand on this ground and the dictionary names both, one on each side. The rebels of 1549 took up arms for the mass, and the doctrine they died for was false; a rising to restore the sacrifice of the altar is not excused by the genuine grievance about an unintelligible English service that stood beside it. But the reprisals were murder done by our side, and the dictionary says so plainly. Kingston's progress through Cornwall, hanging mayors and parish officers without proper trial, was the act of a government that had mistaken slaughter for settlement. Our Lord's rebuke to the disciples who wanted fire called down on a village is the word for it: “Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of” (Luk 9:55).

The second paragraph states the rule that both parties broke. James lays down that the thing a man's anger produces is not the thing God requires, for “the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God” (Jam 1:20), and that holds for the blacksmith marching on Blackheath and for the marshal riding through Cornwall with a rope. Christ's word in the garden settles the method once for all: “Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword” (Mat 26:52), which both the rebels of 1497 and those of 1549 proved in their own persons. And the weapons proper to the cause are named and they are not these: “the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds” (2Co 10:4). A reformation carried by provost marshals was never going to convert a county, and it did not.

“all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword” (Mat 26:52) — An Gof and Flamank at Blackheath, 1497.
“the weapons of our warfare are not carnal” (2Co 10:4) — a reformation carried by provost marshals.

pos: n. (the Cornish castle and gaol town where George Fox was imprisoned in 1656 in the pit called Doomsdale)
etymology: Cornish Lann Stefan, the church enclosure of Stephen, from lann, a church site; the Old English castle name was Dunheved.
biblical_def: Launceston is the Cornish town on the Tamar below the Norman castle of Dunheved, long the county gaol and the seat of the Cornish assizes. Its place in the dictionary is one imprisonment. In 1656 George Fox, with Edward Pyot and William Salt, was taken on the road near St Ives and brought before the justices at Launceston; he refused to remove his hat in court, was fined for contempt and committed, and the three were put into the underground cell called Doomsdale, which Fox describes in his journal as filthy beyond description and never cleaned, where the gaoler charged them for everything and poured the ordure of the prison in upon them. They were held nine weeks until Major-General Desborough had them released. Fox was neither Reformed nor confessional, and the dictionary holds his doctrine of the inner light to be a grave error that puts an immediate illumination in the place of the written Word. It records the gaol all the same, because the treatment of a man for refusing a hat is not answered by the errors in his theology, and because a Protestant magistracy that filled its prisons over such matters was storing up the arguments that would be used against itself.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a gaol as a prison; contempt of court as disobedience to its authority; a dungeon as a dark subterraneous prison; forbearance as the exercise of patience; and testimony as witness borne.
webster_full: GAOL, n. A prison; a place for the confinement of debtors and criminals.
CONTEMPT, n. In law, disobedience to the rules and orders of a court, which is a punishable offence.
DUNGEON, n. A close prison; or a deep dark place of confinement; originally the tower or keep of a castle.
FORBEARANCE, n. The exercise of patience; long suffering; indulgence toward those who injure us.
TESTIMONY, n. A solemn declaration or affirmation made for the purpose of establishing a fact; witness.
scriptures: Act 7:60
And he kneeled down, and cried with a loud voice, Lord, lay not this sin to their charge. And when he had said this, he fell asleep.
Yea, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution.
Joh 16:2
They shall put you out of the synagogues: yea, the time cometh, that whosoever killeth you will think that he doeth God service.
Heb 12:4
Ye have not yet resisted unto blood, striving against sin.
corruption_summary: Cornish gaol town where George Fox and two companions were held nine weeks in 1656 in the underground cell called Doomsdale, committed for refusing to uncover in court.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption named here is ours, and it is the use of the gaol for matters of conscience and ceremony. Fox was committed over a hat; the fine was for contempt and the contempt was his refusal of a gesture he judged to be flattery of men. Whatever is to be said against his theology, and the dictionary says a good deal against it, nothing in it warranted Doomsdale. Our Lord warned His disciples that the men who handled them worst would do it as a service to God, for the time comes “that whosoever killeth you will think that he doeth God service” (Joh 16:2), and that is precisely the temper of a magistracy that gaols men for gestures. Stephen's dying word is the standing pattern for the sufferer, “Lord, lay not this sin to their charge” (Act 7:60).

The second paragraph marks the limits of the sympathy, because the dictionary will not purchase a point against persecution at the price of the doctrine. Fox taught an inner light sufficient for salvation and set it above the Scriptures; the Reformed answer is that the Spirit speaks in and by the Word and never apart from it, and the Quaker scheme, for all its courage under the lash, cut the ground from under preaching and ordinance alike. Both things stand together. Paul tells Timothy that persecution is the ordinary portion of godliness, “all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution” (2Ti 3:12), and the writer to the Hebrews reminds a complaining church of the measure actually taken from it, “Ye have not yet resisted unto blood, striving against sin” (Heb 12:4). An English dissenter reading of Doomsdale in the sixteen-eighties would have found it a nearer prophecy than he liked.

Greek hamartia (G266) — sin, a missing of the mark; “lay not this sin to their charge”, Acts 7:60.
Greek dioko (G1377) — to pursue, to persecute; “shall suffer persecution”, 2 Timothy 3:12.

“Ye have not yet resisted unto blood” (Heb 12:4) — the measure English dissent would soon be given.

pos: n. (the north Cornish headland whose castle and Celtic monastery became the centre of the Arthurian legend)
etymology: Cornish Din Tagell, the fort of the narrow neck, from din, a fort, and a word for a constriction or isthmus.
biblical_def: Tintagel is the headland on the north coast of Cornwall where a narrow neck of rock joins a promontory to the mainland. There was a substantial settlement there in the fifth and sixth centuries, trading in Mediterranean pottery, and a Celtic monastic site on the island; the castle whose ruins stand there now was built by Earl Richard of Cornwall in the twelve-thirties, long after the period to which the legend assigns it. The legend is the point. Geoffrey of Monmouth, writing about 1136, made Tintagel the place of Arthur's conception, and from Geoffrey the whole Arthurian cycle grew, carried on by the French romancers and gathered up by Malory. By the nineteenth century the headland had become a shrine of that literature, and in the twentieth it drew the neo-pagan and the occult trade that still works there. The dictionary records the archaeology, which is real and interesting, and declines the legend, which is fiction presented as history; and it marks the headland as a case of invented tradition hardening into devotion, which is the exact process Scripture forbids in worship.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a legend as a chronicle of a saint's life, hence an incredible story; tradition as the delivery of opinions from father to son; a fable as a feigned story; superstition as excessive exactness in religion; and vain as empty or worthless.
webster_full: LEGEND, n. A chronicle or register of the lives of saints; hence, an idle or incredible story.
TRADITION, n. The delivery of opinions, doctrines, practices or rites from father to son by oral communication.
FABLE, n. A feigned story or tale, intended to instruct or amuse; a fiction; a falsehood.
SUPERSTITION, n. Excessive exactness or rigour in religious opinions or practice; false religion; belief in omens.
VAIN, a. Empty; worthless; having no substance, value or importance; fruitless; ineffectual.
scriptures: Mat 15:9
But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.
What thing soever I command you, observe to do it: thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it.
Col 2:23
Which things have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body; not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh.
Jer 10:5
They are upright as the palm tree, but speak not: they must needs be borne, because they cannot go. Be not afraid of them; for they cannot do evil, neither also is it in them to do good.
corruption_summary: North Cornish headland with a real fifth-century settlement and a Celtic monastic site, made the birthplace of Arthur by Geoffrey of Monmouth about 1136 and a shrine of that invention ever since.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is unusually easy to date. There was a place here, and then in about 1136 a cleric writing a history he largely made up assigned a birth to it, and the assignment has been treated as a fact for eight centuries. The dictionary calls Geoffrey's work what it is, a fable, and notes that the castle shown to visitors was built a hundred years after he wrote and seven centuries after the man he wrote about. Our Lord's verdict on worship built out of such material is exact: “in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men” (Mat 15:9). The rule that would have prevented the whole development is older still and is a rule about addition, “thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it” (Deu 12:32).

The second paragraph names what the headland has become, because the trade there now is not antiquarian. Tintagel draws a steady neo-pagan devotion, with its shops and its ceremonies, and the dictionary declines to treat that as harmless local colour; it is religion offered to nothing. Paul describes the whole class of such observance as having “a shew of wisdom in will worship” (Col 2:23), self-chosen religion that looks impressive and feeds nothing. Jeremiah's mockery of the idol is the right note to end on, and it is a comfort as much as a rebuke: the thing cannot move, cannot speak, and “Be not afraid of them; for they cannot do evil, neither also is it in them to do good” (Jer 10:5). A legend has no power either, and the men who keep it are not to be feared, only told the truth.
